title: Bethune Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Bethune wells have a 248-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $14,700-$25,600.
h1: Bethune, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near Bethune means planning around a real but generally productive plains well. In permits within 5 miles of town, the median reported well depth is 248 feet, and the middle half runs from 220 to 285 feet. Reported yields are also stronger than many buyers expect: the median is 20.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 15.0 to 50.0 gallons per minute.

The records are not complete for every well. Of 363 permits, 158 are recorded as constructed, 218 report total depth, 97 report pump yield, and only 18 report static water level. Use these figures to plan investigation and bidding, not as a guarantee for an unbuilt well.

sections.heading: Bethune well depth: mostly plains drilling below 200 feet
sections.html:
Bethune-area wells are not typically shallow wells. The median reported depth is 248 feet, and half of the wells with reported depths fall between 220 and 285 feet. The deepest record reaches 325 feet. No reported wells are under 100 feet, while 87% fall between 100 and 300 feet and 13% fall between 300 and 600 feet.

The local setting is alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. Permits name the Ogallala in 158 wells and the High Plains Aquifer in 6; 196 name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. For a driller's bid, the middle-half range is more useful than the median alone. A site-specific bid should still account for casing, grout, access, and the formation encountered.

sections.heading: Water yield around Bethune is usually a strong point
sections.html:
Among Bethune-area permits reporting pump yield, the median is 20.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 50.0 gallons per minute, and 89% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 7% fall in the 5 to 15 gallon-per-minute range, while 4% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

That is encouraging for a household or stock use, but yield is not the same as safe daily production. Ask for the actual pump test, recovery information, well construction report, and intended use. An exempt household-use well has a 35 gallon-per-minute pumping limit. Irrigation or other uses may require different water rights, and an augmentation plan can matter in an over-appropriated basin.

sections.heading: Bethune water levels: the available records are limited
sections.html:
Only 18 permits in the local records report a static water level, so the water-level sample is much smaller than the depth sample. Where a level is reported, the median depth to water is 176 feet, and the middle half runs from 160 to 200 feet. That gives a useful planning range for pump setting and trench work, but it does not establish the water level on every parcel.

The permit history does not provide enough comparable water-level measurements by decade to call a declining or stable trend. Do not assume the water table is dropping based on well depth alone. For a purchase, compare nearby well construction reports, request a current static measurement when possible, and have the well and pressure system checked under actual use.

sections.heading: Bethune drilling history shows long local experience
sections.html:
Permits near Bethune span several decades, with 5 issued in the 1950s, 31 in the 1960s, 35 in the 1970s, 15 in the 1980s, 49 in the 1990s, 52 in the 2000s, 17 in the 2010s, and 17 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most frequently listed drillers are Schaal Drilling Co. (Schaal, Ruben T.) with 54 records, Parrish Drilling (Parrish, Wayne) with 44, and Hilt, Fred Jr with 14. Those records show who has appeared most often in the permit data, not who is available or accepting work now. Verify licensing, insurance, references, and the written scope before scheduling.

sections.heading: What a Bethune well may cost to drill and finish
sections.html:
For Bethune's alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the stated drilling rate is $35 to $55 per foot. At the local median depth of 248 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $8,700 to $13,600. That is not the complete water-system price. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $14,700 to $25,600.

Use the median as a comparison point, not a promise. A bid can change with the final depth, casing and grout requirements, access, pump size, power distance, trench conditions, and whether the well needs additional testing or treatment. Ask each driller to separate drilling, casing, development, pump equipment, electrical, trenching, and permits so competing bids can be compared properly.

sections.heading: Bethune risks to check before closing or building
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main pattern in the reported Bethune data, but incomplete records leave room for site-specific problems, including a dry hole or a well that performs poorly under sustained pumping. Have the seller provide the permit, construction report, pump test, water-quality results, and service history. The well's static level and production should be checked rather than inferred from a neighbor.

Environmental review also deserves attention. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 15 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not prove contamination at a particular lot. Test the well for the contaminants relevant to the site and review septic setbacks, building location, access for a rig, and electrical routing before finalizing a plan.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Bethune: use nearby records first
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit file for the parcel and then compare nearby wells in Burlington, Stratton, Vona, Kirk, Seibert, and Joes. Neighbor records can help identify the local formation, likely depth, water level, and driller, but they cannot guarantee the result on your lot. The Bethune data show a typical depth near 248 feet and a typical reported yield of 20.0 gallons per minute.

Before buying, make the contract contingent on a satisfactory well inspection and water test. Before building, confirm the permit allows the intended use, locate the septic system and replacement area, and price the complete water system rather than drilling alone. If the parcel is in an over-appropriated basin, ask Colorado water professionals whether augmentation or another water-rights requirement applies.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Bethune, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Bethune is 248 feet. The middle half runs from 220 to 285 feet. Records show 87% between 100 and 300 feet, 13% between 300 and 600 feet, and none under 100 feet. The deepest recorded well is 325 feet.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Bethune?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 248-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $8,700 to $13,600. A finished system including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $14,700 to $25,600. Actual bids depend on depth, access, construction, and equipment.

faq.q: How much water do Bethune wells produce?
faq.a: Among Bethune-area permits that report a pump yield, the median is 20.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 15.0 to 50.0 gallons per minute, and 89% report more than 15 gallons per minute. These are permit-record results, not a guarantee for a new well, so request a pump test and recovery information.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Bethune?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that every Bethune well is safe to drink. The mapped area within about 10 miles has 15 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well for site-relevant contaminants, bacteria, and other drinking-water concerns, and review the result with a qualified water professional.

faq.q: Should I test a Bethune well before buying property?
faq.a: Yes. Only 18 local permits report a static water level, and only 97 report a pump yield, so the records are incomplete. Request the permit, construction report, pump test, static level, and water-quality results. Compare neighboring wells, but inspect and test the actual property because a nearby 248-foot median does not guarantee the same result.
